clue.text: Small poet taking taxi gets protection on the side

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a cab is a taxi
a bard is a poet, as Shakespeare is the Bard

explanation.surface: A minor poet hails a taxi and gets some sort of protection on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' is only a link: the three pieces simply follow one another.
explanation.definitionFit: A sword is sheathed in its holder worn at the hip, guarding the blade and the wearer.

clue.text: Macho sort misused internet facilities

indicators.note: misused says the letters of the two words before it are put to a wrong arrangement

explanation.surface: A he-man type has been abusing online services.
explanation.definitionFit: Online venues where users exchange typed messages in real time are web services of this kind.

clue.text: Beat established for an audience

indicators.note: for an audience says the word is to be heard spoken, not seen written

parts.note: established means based, as in a firm based in London

explanation.surface: A rhythm already set up for the listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' looks like a musical noun, but it is the verb: to thrash someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrash or cudgel someone soundly is an old sense of this verb, besides moistening a roast.

clue.text: Flying clearance needed by party for faster passage

indicators.note: Flying says the letters of the word after it are sent all over the place

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A flight clearance is required at a party for a quick getaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needed by' is a link joining the anagram ACCELERAN (from 'clearance', shuffled by 'Flying') to DO.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical direction meaning gradually speeding up, so a stretch of music played increasingly fast.

clue.text: Where it's not lively, in the main?

definitions.text: Where it's not lively, in the main?

parts.words: Where it's not lively, in the main?
parts.note: the main is the sea, and a body of salt water where nothing lives is one without life in it

explanation.walkthrough: 'in the main' looks like 'mostly', but the main is an old word for the sea; this salt lake between Israel and Jordan supports no fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A salt lake so briny that fish cannot survive in it is lifeless water, a 'sea' with nothing living.

clue.text: Pub with English setting

parts.note: a local is one's neighbourhood pub

explanation.surface: A pub with an English backdrop.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the local' is the pub nearest home.
explanation.definitionFit: A place where events happen, the scene of a story or action, is its setting.

clue.text: Shaver cut woman

indicators.note: cut says the word before it loses its final letter

parts.note: a lady is a woman

explanation.surface: A razor nicked a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shaver' suggests a razor, but a 'young shaver' is an old word for a boy; 'cut' docks the Y from LADY.
explanation.definitionFit: A young shaver is dated slang for a youngster or boy.

clue.text: Rocky ascent is nothing for these travellers?

indicators.note: Rocky says the letters are unsteady and must be rearranged

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Paddlers think nothing of a climb over rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky' looks like part of the landscape, but it signals the anagram of ASCENT IS plus O.
explanation.definitionFit: People who paddle small light boats along rivers are a kind of water traveller.

clue.text: Pick up large gain

parts.note: to earn is to gain money

explanation.surface: Collect a big profit.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick up a skill or language is to acquire knowledge of it.

clue.text: Style of GBS writing is better

definitions.meaning: initials such as GBS (George Bernard Shaw) are written in upper-case letters
to top or outdo something is to go one better than it

explanation.surface: Shaw's prose style is superior.
explanation.walkthrough: GBS looks like Shaw's style, but it only illustrates capital letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Upper-case lettering is the form initials take, and to outdo or surpass something is to go one better.

clue.text: Wine daily? Academic gets negative

parts.note: a daily, or char, is a British cleaning woman who comes in each day
a don is a university teacher
nay is an old word for no

explanation.surface: A cleaner asks whether wine is a daily thing; the professor says no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daily' looks like an adverb about drinking habits, but in Britain a daily (or char) is a cleaning lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A popular dry white grape variety and the drink made from it.

clue.text: British novelist offering an alternative to spring

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
a well is a spring of water

explanation.surface: A British writer proposes something other than a spring.
explanation.definitionFit: George, author of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, was an English writer of fiction.

clue.text: Pepper, say, prepared around hot range

indicators.note: around says the first word's letters go about the outside of the rest

parts.note: set means prepared, as in all set

indicators.note: hot means agitated, so the letters of the next word are stirred up

explanation.surface: Pepper is ready to go on a hot cooking stove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pepper' looks like seasoning by the range, but it is Sgt Pepper of the Beatles album; 'hot' is an unusual anagram signal, meaning agitated, and 'around' puts SET about the result.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beatles' Sgt Pepper is a fictional example of this military rank.

clue.text: Call before golf tournament for performance directors

indicators.note: before places the call's word ahead of the tournament's

parts.note: to ring is to call on the telephone
the Masters is a major golf championship played at Augusta

explanation.surface: Phone ahead of a golf championship to reach the people running the show.
explanation.definitionFit: Circus officials who announce and direct the acts under the big top.

clue.text: Without doubt power drill right to be put first

parts.note: force means power

indicators.note: to be put first says the right letter moves to the front of its word

parts.note: to train is to drill, as soldiers are drilled

explanation.surface: A power drill, sure enough, needs its proper setting first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'power drill' looks like one tool, but it splits into two pieces; 'to be put first' moves the R to the front of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase meaning surely or definitely, said of something known beyond question.

clue.text: Musical drama in shelter gets band together

indicators.note: in says the drama sits inside the word for shelter

parts.note: a cote is a small shelter for doves or sheep
an opera is a drama set to music

explanation.surface: An opera put on in a shed brings the band together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' looks like a group of musicians, fitting the opera, but here it is the verb to unite; 'gets' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To work jointly with others towards a shared end is to unite or collaborate.

clue.text: Fair call for aid with oxygen

parts.note: SOS is the distress signal
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A fairly reasonable plea for help with breathing gas.
explanation.definitionFit: Middling or passable, neither good nor bad, is what fair can mean.

clue.text: Who may be working in Dover and tees?

definitions.text: Who may be working in Dover and tees?

indicators.note: working says the letters of Dover and tees are set in motion and rearranged

explanation.surface: Who might be employed at Dover docks or on Teesside?
explanation.walkthrough: Dover and the Tees are both ports, so a docker fits the whole clue; 'working' signals the anagram, and Tees (the river) is disguised in lower case.
explanation.definitionFit: A dock labourer who loads and unloads ships, as one might at a port like Dover.

clue.text: Court order, for instance given to lad endlessly?

parts.note: as means for instance, as in 'big cats, as lions'

indicators.note: endlessly says the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a boy is a lad

explanation.surface: A court order, for example, handed to a young lad who never stops.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an ASBO was an Anti-Social Behaviour Order, often imposed on rowdy youths, so the lad fits the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A British anti-social behaviour order was a civil injunction issued by magistrates.

clue.text: Girls mean to be first in flying incidents

indicators.note: to be first says the word for mean goes ahead of the word for girls

parts.note: near is a dated British word for mean or stingy
misses are young women

explanation.surface: Girls intend to lead when there are aerial mishaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mean' looks like 'intend', but it is the adjective stingy, which near meant in old British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Two aircraft coming dangerously close without colliding are aviation scares.

clue.text: One jolly group getting support for member

parts.note: one is the article a
a jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
a band is a group

explanation.surface: A cheerful band finds backing for one of its members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jolly' looks like an adjective for the group, but it is slang for a Royal Marine; 'member' is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflatable band worn on the upper arm keeps a learner swimmer afloat, supporting that limb.

clue.text: Back secured by cable in the morning, left space

indicators.note: Back says the whole run of letters that follows is read in reverse

parts.note: a boat moored is tied up with ropes or cables
AM means before noon

explanation.surface: A boat tied up at the back early in the day, leaving room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns the whole of MOOREDAM around.
explanation.definitionFit: To clear an area so that someone or something can fit is to vacate space.

clue.text: What's quickly seen in recurrent spare capacity

indicators.note: recurrent says the hidden letters are read backwards
seen in says the letters are found within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Speed visible in a repeated surplus of capacity.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'What's quickly seen' as the definition, leaving no hidden-word indicator; 'quickly' alone defines, and 'seen in' signals the hidden run, 'What's' being a link.
explanation.definitionFit: At a swift rate or with speed, as in work progressing fast.

clue.text: Great sandwiches first in pub meal

indicators.note: sandwiches says the first word holds the next piece between its letters

parts.note: super means great

indicators.note: first in picks out the opening letter of the word after it

explanation.surface: A great meal in the pub starts with sandwiches.
explanation.definitionFit: An evening repast, the last of the day.

clue.text: What you get from a hot dog is rubbish

definitions.text: What you get from a hot dog
definitions.meaning: an overheated dog breathes heavily with its tongue out
British slang for nonsense or something of poor quality

explanation.surface: Something from a hot dog proves to be worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hot dog' looks like a sausage in a bun, but it is a dog feeling the heat; the British slang sense is 'that's rubbish'.
explanation.definitionFit: A warm dog breathes in short gasps, and British slang uses the same word for something worthless.

clue.text: Selling at home, Georgia gets angry and bitter

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
rages means gets angry
bitter is a type of British beer, an ale

explanation.surface: A home sale in Georgia leaves someone angry and resentful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bitter' looks like a feeling, but it is the British pale beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Disposing of unwanted household goods from one's own property, usually laid out on the driveway.

clue.text: Lamb, partly stewed

indicators.note: partly says only a portion of the next word is used

explanation.surface: Lamb, partially casseroled.
explanation.walkthrough: Stewed lamb is a kitchen scene, but 'Lamb' here is a young female sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: A female lamb is a female sheep from birth, so a young one still counts.

clue.text: An element disheartened, never let on

indicators.note: disheartened says the phrase that follows loses its whole central stretch, keeping only its two ends

explanation.surface: Someone discouraged keeps their feelings to themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disheartened' looks like a mood, but it strips the middle five letters VERLET from NEVERLETON, leaving the outer NE and ON; an unusually large heart to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: A noble gas used in glowing advertising signs is one of the chemical elements.

clue.text: Cut on end of nose is serious

parts.note: to sever is to cut

indicators.note: end of picks out the final letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A cut on the tip of the nose is a grave matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave or harsh, as an illness or punishment can be.

clue.text: What asteroids could produce, nothing less

definitions.text: What asteroids could produce, nothing less

indicators.note: could produce says the letters of asteroids are worked into something new
less says the letter for nothing is taken away

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Asteroids could cause a catastrophe, no less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less' removes the O from ASTEROIDS, and 'could produce' rearranges the rest; an asteroid strike is itself a catastrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: A catastrophe is what an asteroid strike on Earth would bring.
